title: Congratulations and holidays
goal: Congratulate people, give gifts, and get to know the two holidays that bring all of Korea to a halt — while adding the particle 에게/한테, which hasn't been practiced until now.
bekal: congratulating people on birthdays and achievements
using 에게 and 한테 to mark the recipient
telling 주다 apart from 드리다 and 받다
recognizing 설날 and 추석 and their greetings

dialogs.title: 대화 — Suji's birthday
dialogs.intro: Ani arrives with a gift. Notice that giving to an equal uses a different verb from giving to someone older.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Oh, thank you! How did you know?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Minjun told me. This is a little gift.
lines.literal: Minjun — Mr. — subject — tell — gave. this — small — gift — is.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Oh, you shouldn't have… Can I open it?
lines.literal: what — this-kind — thing — all… open — try-even-if — okay?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes, go ahead and open it. It's Indonesian coffee.
lines.literal: yes, open — try. Indonesia — coffee — is.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Wow, thank you so much! I really love coffee.
lines.literal: wow, truly — thank-you! coffee — really — like.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: I'm glad. Did you give your parents a gift too?
lines.literal: glad — is. parents-to — also — gift — gave (humble)?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Yes, I gave my mother flowers. On our birthday we thank our parents.
lines.literal: yes, mother-to — flowers — object — gave (humble). birthday-on — as-for — parents-to — thanks — greeting — object — give (humble).

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Oh, really? That's different from Indonesia.
lines.literal: ah, so — is? Indonesia — with — different — I-see.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Yes. Because we're grateful they gave birth to us.
lines.literal: yes. give-birth — gave (honorific) — so — grateful — because — polite.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: What a lovely custom. Have you had seaweed soup?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Of course! My mom made it for me this morning.
lines.literal: of-course! morning-in — mom — subject — boil — gave (honorific).

notes: **축하해요 is used for all congratulations**, not just birthdays: 생일 축하해요, 졸업 축하해요, 결혼 축하해요, 합격 축하해요. The formal version is 축하드립니다, which is what you use with a boss.

**에게 and 한테 mean the same, with a different tone.** Both mean "to" for people or animals. 한테 is spoken and everyday; 에게 is a bit more written. ⚠️ For things and places, use **에**, not 에게: 회사**에** 전화했어요 (I called the office).
**께 is the honorific form of 에게.** 어머니**께** 드렸어요 = I gave it to my mother. It pairs with the humble verb 드리다, and the two must appear together — using 께 with 줬어요 sounds half-finished.

**주다 and 드리다 both mean "to give", and the choice depends on the recipient.** 친구**한테** **줬어요** (gave to a friend) but 부모님**께** **드렸어요** (gave to my parents). A direct application of the humble forms in unit 18: you lower your own action to raise the recipient.

**-아/어 주다 means doing something for someone.** 알려 **줬어요** = told (me, as a favor). 끓여 **주셨어요** = cooked (for me, by someone respected). It's the same pattern you've used in 주세요 since unit 10 — now in the past and honorific forms.

**뭐 이런 걸 다… is the expected polite protest.** Said when receiving a gift, it means roughly "oh, you shouldn't have". Accepting a gift without a little token protest is seen as slightly impolite — and the giver is expecting this line.

**In Korea, gifts are often not opened in front of the giver**, especially in formal situations. That's why Suji asks 열어 봐도 돼요? first. Between close friends, opening it right away is perfectly normal.

**미역국 is the must-have birthday soup.** Seaweed is believed to help mothers recover after giving birth, so eating it on your birthday is a way of remembering the day you were born. ⚠️ For the same reason, eating it on an exam day is bad luck: 미역 is slippery, and you might "slip" on your exam.

grammars.title: To whom: 에게, 한테, 께
body: Three forms for one role, told apart by who the recipient is and how formal the sentence is.
after: **Verbs that pair with these particles:** 주다 (give), 드리다 (give, humble), 받다 (receive), 보내다 (send), 전화하다 (call), 말하다 (say), 가르치다 (teach), 물어보다 (ask).
⚠️ **말하다 takes 한테 for the person, not 을/를.** 친구**한테** 말했어요 = I told my friend. 친구를 말했어요 means "I talked about my friend (as a topic)" — something else entirely.

grammars.title: Giving, receiving, and doing for others
body: Three verbs circling one idea, and two of them change form depending on who's on the other side.
after: **도와드릴까요? ("may I help you?") is a phrase you'll hear often in shops and on the street.** It combines 돕다 + -아 드리다 + -(으)ㄹ까요, and you've learned every part of it.
**Korean pays close attention to the direction of giving**, far more than English does. A sentence that's grammatically correct but has the direction wrong sounds odd, even if every word is right.

blocks.text: Two holidays that bring all of Korea to a halt

head: 설날
추석
rows: Go back to their hometown, 세배 (a deep bow to elders)
Go back to their hometown, visit ancestors' graves
Everyone travels at once — the highways jam completely

blocks.text: **떡국 has a special meaning**: eating it on 설날 means you've grown one year older. It's a leftover of the old age system explained in unit 8 — in Korea, everyone used to turn a year older together at New Year, not on their own birthday.

blocks.title: Writing a greeting message
items: **To a friend:** 생일 축하해요! 좋은 하루 보내세요 ㅎㅎ
**To a boss or teacher:** 생신 축하드립니다. 항상 건강하세요. — note 생신, the honorific form of 생일.
**New Year, to anyone:** 새해 복 많이 받으세요. 올해도 잘 부탁드립니다.
⚠️ Greetings to older people almost always use **-드립니다** and **-(으)세요**, never casual forms. When in doubt, copy the second example above.

exercises.prompt: Fill in 한테, 께 or 에.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: 생일 축하해요! — 이거 작은 선물이에요. — 열어 봐도 돼요? — 어머니께 꽃을 드렸어요. — 새해 복 많이 받으세요. — 건강하세요.
수지 씨 생일 축하해요. — 이거 작은 선물이에요. — 열어 봐도 돼요? — 어머니께 꽃을 드렸어요. — 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
